items.title: AI Models Can Name Anonymous Reviewers and Redditors From a Single Text
items.summary: Give a frontier AI model one anonymous text, ask who wrote it, and it will often give you a name. No web search, no list of suspects. That is the finding of a preprint that twelve researchers from the University of Maryland, Simon Fraser University, the University of British Columbia, Pangram Labs and Google DeepMind posted on arXiv on 19 November and revised on 23 November. The strongest model they tested, Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2, named the reviewer of 55% of 15,136 peer reviews from the ICML 2020 machine-learning conference. Neither the reviews nor their authors were ever made public. It also named the account behind 69% of comments by Reddit users who had posted or commented more than 500 times in that subreddit over the past year. The paper hasn’t been peer reviewed yet. Its authors conclude that anyone who has published enough writing online can no longer assume an unsigned text keeps them anonymous, and that defences are limited. Disclosure: this article was researched and drafted with Claude Opus 5.5, one of the models the study tests, and reviewed by its author before publication. Anthropic makes both Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2, the study’s best performer. PrivacyAffairs pays for a Claude subscription and has no other tie to Anthropic, which had no input.

items.title: Fake Italian Interior Ministry App Spied on Asylum Seekers
items.summary: An Android app dressed up as an Italian Interior Ministry service told asylum seekers it had news about their protection status. It was spyware. The investigative outlet IrpiMedia published the findings on 27 November. Reporter Rosita Rijtano started from analyses by the mobile security firm Lookout, which found the app in 2024, and an independent researcher confirmed and extended them. They trace the spyware to IPS, a surveillance company headquartered in Aprilia, in the province of Latina, that sells to Italian prosecutors, police and intelligence agencies. IrpiMedia could not establish whose phones the app reached, or whether it served an intelligence operation or a criminal investigation. IPS and the Interior and Justice ministries did not answer its questions. We looked up the domain that served the app. Its registry record names the same small company that researchers found behind an earlier campaign with the same spyware, and someone is still renewing it.

items.title: How Long Does It Take to Read a Privacy Policy? We Measured the 100 Most Visited Sites (2026)
items.summary: About 27 minutes for a typical one. Reading all 84 privacy policies behind the 100 most visited websites in the US would take 41 and a half hours, a full working week. We collected every policy on 28 November 2026, counted the words, timed them at an average adult reading speed and scored how hard they are to read. Then we pulled the same companies’ policies from early 2018, before the GDPR deadline, to see how they changed. The full table is in chapter 7, and the data is a free CSV download. Key findings 27 minutes is what a typical privacy policy takes to read: the median of the 84 policies is 6,353 words. 41.5 hours to read all 84, a full working week. The 16 policies behind the 20 most visited sites alone take 9 hours. Microsoft has the longest: 32,456 words, 2 hours and 16 minutes. Fourteen policies pass 10,000 words. 0 of 84 reach plain English on the Flesch scale; 83 score at college level or harder. 2.1 times as long as in early 2018: the median of the 48 policies we could compare went from 2,941 to 6,260 words. 29 of 84 say they use, or may use, your data to train AI or machine-learning models. In early 2018, none of 48 did.

items.title: 1Password data breach included some customer info, internal source code
items.summary: 1Password is reassuring customers that their password vaults are safe after the theft of both account records for a subset of its users and source code from its private repositories. The company said it began investigating the incident on November 19, after it detected indications that an employee’s corporate GitHub account had been breached. The attacker used the account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, which downloaded what 1Password described as “administrative data” about a subset of users. This included customer names and email addresses, account and user IDs, account creation and last sign-in times, public keys, Secure Remote Password protocol parameters, and “other non-secret account metadata relative to our internal architecture.” Tokens used in some emailed links to customers inviting them to accept provisioning invitations or account recovery were also stolen, although 1Password said that these tokens must be combined with an SSO sign-in or a six-digit confirmation code sent to the user’s registered email address before account access is granted. The company has notified affected customers and, to further secure authentication, has changed the confirmation code format from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric characters. The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and accessed the continuous integration/continuous delivery (CI/CD) system; while 1Password said that the source code contained no user secrets, infrastructure secrets in the CI/CD system may have been exposed. The company has triggered a rotation of all relevant credentials. Vaults not affected However, it emphasized, customers’ password vaults were not affected, nor were the keys that protect them. The company also pointed out that it does not store account passwords or secret keys; customers are the only ones who have keys to their vaults. Account recovery keys and 1Password apps and browser extensions are also safe, it said. Actions taken 1Password said that, in response to the breach, as well performing the credential rotation and lengthening of confirmation codes, it has disabled the compromised GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, and removed the access created by the attacker. It also has tightened internal controls on GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoints and added new detections for attacks such as this. Finally, it checked for internal evidence of user account takeovers or compromise, and has brought in independent cybersecurity experts to validate its efforts. Recommendations for customers In its post, 1Password warned customers to beware of phishing attacks in the wake of this incident and reminded them that it will never contact them to ask for account passwords or Secret Keys. “Only enter them in the official 1Password app, or on our official website, and only when you’ve opened the app or typed the address yourself. Your Secret Key is only needed the first time you sign in on a new device or browser,” it advised. Fritz Jean-Louis , principal cybersecurity instructor at Infotech, also recommended that customers monitor for suspicious activity, particularly phishing attempts that exploit concerns about the breach, adding that security teams should pay close attention to unexpected account recovery requests and unusual account provisioning activity as well. He noted that, although this is a serious breach of 1Password’s backend environment, it is somewhat mitigated by the fact that, according to the company, there is no evidence that customer password vaults were compromised. “For organizations using the service, that distinction is important,” he said. “Some customer account information was affected, but the vaults containing passwords and secrets were not reported to have been accessed. Based on the information disclosed so far, I do not see a need for a blanket reset of passwords stored in those vaults solely because of this incident.” This is also a good opportunity for organizations to review all of their identity and access monitoring, he added. “Organizations should verify that their security information and event management system is monitoring those activities and providing meaningful alerts,” he said. “Even where a third party handles that monitoring, it is worth checking that the right coverage is in place.”

items.title: Cybercriminals Use Stolen API Credentials to Book ₹2.15 Crore Flight Tickets in Mumbai
items.summary: A significant financial fraud in Mumbai highlights the vulnerability of corporate systems in India to cybercriminals. Corporate Systems Cybersecurity Incident Corporate systems in India have become a focal point for cybercriminals, as evidenced by a significant financial fraud in Mumbai involving the unauthorized use of travel agency credentials. A travel company based in Goregaon suffered losses exceeding Rs 2.15 crore after attackers exploited its API connections to book 38 international flights without authorization. Compromised Organization and API Usage The compromised organization, which serves approximately 30,000 customers annually and holds an International Air Transport Association (IATA) license, utilizes API credentials provided by a Bengaluru-based technology vendor to interface with airline reservation systems. These credentials enable the agency to perform real-time seat checks, fare comparisons, and ticket processing across multiple carriers. The company maintains a Rs 1 crore credit facility for ticket purchases, which the attackers leveraged to their advantage. Unauthorized Activity Discovery The unauthorized activity was identified on November 9 during a routine system review by the company’s IT department. Initial findings revealed five international tickets with recorded payments of Rs 32.69 lakh, but these transactions lacked standard agent identifiers or reference numbers. Further investigation uncovered 33 additional tickets booked between November 6 and 9 under 21 separate Passenger Name Records (PNRs), with a total value of Rs 2.15 crore. The affected airlines included carriers operating from France, Qatar, Turkey, and the United Arab Emirates. Evidence of Concealment Evidence suggests the perpetrators attempted to conceal their activities within the booking system. Following one unsuccessful transaction attempt, related data was systematically deleted, which likely delayed detection of the breach. The company confirmed that no legitimate authorization had been issued for these bookings. Immediate Response and Investigation Upon discovering the irregularities, the agency immediately notified its Bengaluru-based technical provider, and both entities conducted a joint forensic examination. The audit confirmed unauthorized access to the API credentials. The incident was subsequently reported to India’s national cybercrime reporting portal 1930, and a formal police complaint was filed. Financial Repercussions The financial repercussions extended beyond the initial fraudulent bookings. Six of the 38 tickets had already been utilized by passengers before the fraud was detected. When the travel agency attempted to cancel the remaining 32 tickets, the airlines imposed cancellation penalties totaling approximately Rs 60 lakh. Law Enforcement Investigation Law enforcement authorities are currently investigating the methods used to compromise the API credentials, examining potential security vulnerabilities, procedural oversights, or other attack vectors. The investigation will also include passenger records and financial transaction trails to identify the criminal network behind the scheme. Cybersecurity Recommendations Cybersecurity specialists have highlighted the risks associated with static API credentials, recommending periodic rotation of access keys and implementation of strict usage policies. Additional protective measures include restricting API access to designated network environments, deploying automated blocking for suspicious access attempts, and implementing real-time monitoring systems that flag unusual booking patterns or high-value transactions. Broader Implications This incident underscores the growing targeting of technical infrastructure supporting corporate booking platforms, emphasizing that API security controls are as critical to business operations as traditional financial safeguards.

A significant financial fraud in Mumbai highlights the vulnerability of corporate systems in India to cybercriminals.

Corporate Systems Cybersecurity Incident

Corporate systems in India have become a focal point for cybercriminals, as evidenced by a significant financial fraud in Mumbai involving the unauthorized use of travel agency credentials. A travel company based in Goregaon suffered losses exceeding Rs 2.15 crore after attackers exploited its API connections to book 38 international flights without authorization.

Compromised Organization and API Usage

The compromised organization, which serves approximately 30,000 customers annually and holds an International Air Transport Association (IATA) license, utilizes API credentials provided by a Bengaluru-based technology vendor to interface with airline reservation systems. These credentials enable the agency to perform real-time seat checks, fare comparisons, and ticket processing across multiple carriers. The company maintains a Rs 1 crore credit facility for ticket purchases, which the attackers leveraged to their advantage.

Unauthorized Activity Discovery

The unauthorized activity was identified on November 9 during a routine system review by the company’s IT department. Initial findings revealed five international tickets with recorded payments of Rs 32.69 lakh, but these transactions lacked standard agent identifiers or reference numbers. Further investigation uncovered 33 additional tickets booked between November 6 and 9 under 21 separate Passenger Name Records (PNRs), with a total value of Rs 2.15 crore. The affected airlines included carriers operating from France, Qatar, Turkey, and the United Arab Emirates.

Evidence of Concealment

Evidence suggests the perpetrators attempted to conceal their activities within the booking system. Following one unsuccessful transaction attempt, related data was systematically deleted, which likely delayed detection of the breach. The company confirmed that no legitimate authorization had been issued for these bookings.

Immediate Response and Investigation

Upon discovering the irregularities, the agency immediately notified its Bengaluru-based technical provider, and both entities conducted a joint forensic examination. The audit confirmed unauthorized access to the API credentials. The incident was subsequently reported to India’s national cybercrime reporting portal 1930, and a formal police complaint was filed.

Financial Repercussions

The financial repercussions extended beyond the initial fraudulent bookings. Six of the 38 tickets had already been utilized by passengers before the fraud was detected. When the travel agency attempted to cancel the remaining 32 tickets, the airlines imposed cancellation penalties totaling approximately Rs 60 lakh.

Law Enforcement Investigation

Law enforcement authorities are currently investigating the methods used to compromise the API credentials, examining potential security vulnerabilities, procedural oversights, or other attack vectors. The investigation will also include passenger records and financial transaction trails to identify the criminal network behind the scheme.

Cybersecurity Recommendations

Cybersecurity specialists have highlighted the risks associated with static API credentials, recommending periodic rotation of access keys and implementation of strict usage policies. Additional protective measures include restricting API access to designated network environments, deploying automated blocking for suspicious access attempts, and implementing real-time monitoring systems that flag unusual booking patterns or high-value transactions.

Broader Implications

This incident underscores the growing targeting of technical infrastructure supporting corporate booking platforms, emphasizing that API security controls are as critical to business operations as traditional financial safeguards.

items.title: Does a VPN Slow Down Your Internet? What 8 VPNs Did to My Speed, and How to Fix a Slow One
items.summary: Yes, a little. Eight VPNs kept about 88% of my download speed on a nearby server, and about 70% on a server on the other side of the world. The download is rarely what you notice, though. Distance hurts ping and upload much more, and the wrong protocol can take away nine-tenths of your speed. That last part is the easy one to fix. I tested ExpressVPN, NordVPN, Surfshark, PIA, CyberGhost, Proton VPN, Mullvad and Amnezia VPN on 23 and 24 November 2026 for our reviews, all on the same laptop and line. Every number on this page without another source comes from those tests. items.title: VPN Not Connecting or Keeps Dropping? Find the Cause and Fix It
items.summary: When a VPN won’t connect, the cause is usually the network you’re on or something on your own device. Four quick tests tell you which. Most troubleshooting lists are written by VPN companies and end with a reason to install their app. This one is sorted by what you actually see, because “won’t connect”, “connected but nothing loads”, “keeps dropping” and “no internet since I turned it off” have different causes, and the fix for one can make another worse. A VPN that only works with its leak protection off isn’t working. Settings, menu names and help pages checked on the providers’ and platforms’ own sites on 28 November 2026.

items.title: Fake Government App Exposes Italy’s Expanding Spyware Surveillance Industry
items.summary: A fake Interior Ministry app used Morpheus spyware to target asylum seekers in Italy, raising questions about surveillance and oversight. An Android app called FirmaDigitale promised asylum seekers news on their protection status, instead, it was delivering spyware. An IrpiMedia investigation by Rosita Rijtano builds on Lookout’s 2024 discovery and attributes the malware to IPS, a Latina supplier to prosecutors, police and intelligence agencies. Nobody knows who ordered the operation or whom it hit. Victims downloaded the app from firmadigitale.assistenza-mobile[.]it, a page mimicking the website of Italy’s primary postal service provider Poste Italiane. The app displayed the Interior Ministry logo and mentioned a protection decree. Police deny any link to it, and Poste didn’t comment. The spyware could add components to use the microphone, intercept internet calls, record the screen and track the phone. It could also reach contacts, call logs, files and texts. The site has been unreachable since 2025, but the app could still circulate elsewhere. Osservatorio Nessuno named the spyware Morpheus in April 2026 after finding it in a fake Fastweb app. Attackers also abused the TIM, Iliad, PosteMobile and WindTre brands, and Iliad said it knew of no such apps. Morpheus can even hijack WhatsApp through a fake biometric prompt. “We are faced with yet another example of low-cost spyware that exploits vulnerability and suffering to strike at one of every individual’s most intimate rights: the privacy of the devices we use daily for all our activities and communications,” comments a spokesperson for Osservatorio Nessuno , a volunteer organization that studies digital surveillance technologies and provides technical assistance to journalists and activists. “This case is particularly cruel because it leverages—from a position of supreme power—systems that are already discriminatory and hostile, specifically targeting migrants. The responsibility lies in many quarters: from the complete lack of Italian or European regulation regarding the proliferation of such companies, to a total absence of transparency and constraints—including ethical ones—on these types of operations.” Kristina Balaam of Citizen Lab, formerly at Lookout, says social engineering makes these tools cheaper than zero-click spyware and still effective. Why burn a rare exploit when a convincing form will do? Osservatorio Nessuno blames weak Italian and European rules, opacity and missing ethical limits. Civil liberties coalition Cild wants to know why authorities would target asylum seekers, who authorized it and what it produced. IPS has plenty of company, including RCS, Area, SIO and Innova. Nine established firms reported €214.4 million in 2024 revenue from surveillance and intelligence tools. Italy supplied 72.8% of revenue among the five disclosing geography. Spyware targets rose from 2,894 in 2021 to 5,611 in 2025, up about 94%. Mafia cases accounted for 2,930 last year, ordinary crimes for 2,618 and terrorism for 63. Germany authorized 91 spyware operations in 2024 and carried out 57. Italian law permits spyware well beyond mafia and terrorism cases, including corruption and many ordinary crimes. Defence lawyer Eugenio Losco warns that a criminal association charge opens the door, even against unionists and activists. Interception spending also reached about €299 million in 2025, despite a national price list meant to cut costs. Controls remain thin. Italy has no prior quality check, and authorities lack the skills to verify the software. In the eSurv case, a company kept intercepts on its own servers, and its trial continues. Magistrates’ association vice president Marcello De Chiara calls spyware essential and current safeguards for its use adequate. He wants tighter rules for private vendors, including a national register and clearer ownership. The concern extends beyond this app. A researcher says at least five activists recently received spyware links, while Sea-Watch’s Giorgia Linardi has reported zero-click surveillance in 2021. IrpiMedia doesn’t tie either case to FirmaDigitale. Lawyer Giovanni Battista Gallus says Italy lacks a complete law limiting what spyware can do. Collected data can remain archived, and authorities needn’t notify targets when an investigation is shelved. IrpiMedia captures the result, that targets may never find out, in one sentence: “Those who are spied upon may never even find out. In fact, there is no obligation to notify an individual that they have been subjected to surveillance once an investigation is closed.” Gallus concludes. “Furthermore, while the surveillance tools must be deactivated at the end of an operation, the material collected is not automatically deleted; instead, it may remain stored in the public prosecutor’s archives.” Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon Pierluigi Paganini ( SecurityAffairs – hacking, Morpheus spyware)

A fake Interior Ministry app used Morpheus spyware to target asylum seekers in Italy, raising questions about surveillance and oversight.

An Android app called FirmaDigitale promised asylum seekers news on their protection status, instead, it was delivering spyware.

An IrpiMedia investigation by Rosita Rijtano builds on Lookout’s 2024 discovery and attributes the malware to IPS, a Latina supplier to prosecutors, police and intelligence agencies. Nobody knows who ordered the operation or whom it hit.

Victims downloaded the app from firmadigitale.assistenza-mobile[.]it, a page mimicking the website of Italy’s primary postal service provider Poste Italiane. The app displayed the Interior Ministry logo and mentioned a protection decree. Police deny any link to it, and Poste didn’t comment.

The spyware could add components to use the microphone, intercept internet calls, record the screen and track the phone. It could also reach contacts, call logs, files and texts. The site has been unreachable since 2025, but the app could still circulate elsewhere.

Osservatorio Nessuno named the spyware Morpheus in April 2026 after finding it in a fake Fastweb app. Attackers also abused the TIM, Iliad, PosteMobile and WindTre brands, and Iliad said it knew of no such apps. Morpheus can even hijack WhatsApp through a fake biometric prompt.

“We are faced with yet another example of low-cost spyware that exploits vulnerability and suffering to strike at one of every individual’s most intimate rights: the privacy of the devices we use daily for all our activities and communications,” comments a spokesperson for Osservatorio Nessuno, a volunteer organization that studies digital surveillance technologies and provides technical assistance to journalists and activists.

“This case is particularly cruel because it leverages—from a position of supreme power—systems that are already discriminatory and hostile, specifically targeting migrants. The responsibility lies in many quarters: from the complete lack of Italian or European regulation regarding the proliferation of such companies, to a total absence of transparency and constraints—including ethical ones—on these types of operations.”

Kristina Balaam of Citizen Lab, formerly at Lookout, says social engineering makes these tools cheaper than zero-click spyware and still effective. Why burn a rare exploit when a convincing form will do?

Osservatorio Nessuno blames weak Italian and European rules, opacity and missing ethical limits. Civil liberties coalition Cild wants to know why authorities would target asylum seekers, who authorized it and what it produced.

IPS has plenty of company, including RCS, Area, SIO and Innova. Nine established firms reported €214.4 million in 2024 revenue from surveillance and intelligence tools. Italy supplied 72.8% of revenue among the five disclosing geography.

Spyware targets rose from 2,894 in 2021 to 5,611 in 2025, up about 94%. Mafia cases accounted for 2,930 last year, ordinary crimes for 2,618 and terrorism for 63. Germany authorized 91 spyware operations in 2024 and carried out 57.

Italian law permits spyware well beyond mafia and terrorism cases, including corruption and many ordinary crimes. Defence lawyer Eugenio Losco warns that a criminal association charge opens the door, even against unionists and activists. Interception spending also reached about €299 million in 2025, despite a national price list meant to cut costs.

Controls remain thin. Italy has no prior quality check, and authorities lack the skills to verify the software. In the eSurv case, a company kept intercepts on its own servers, and its trial continues.

Magistrates’ association vice president Marcello De Chiara calls spyware essential and current safeguards for its use adequate. He wants tighter rules for private vendors, including a national register and clearer ownership.

The concern extends beyond this app. A researcher says at least five activists recently received spyware links, while Sea-Watch’s Giorgia Linardi has reported zero-click surveillance in 2021. IrpiMedia doesn’t tie either case to FirmaDigitale.

Lawyer Giovanni Battista Gallus says Italy lacks a complete law limiting what spyware can do. Collected data can remain archived, and authorities needn’t notify targets when an investigation is shelved. IrpiMedia captures the result, that targets may never find out, in one sentence:

“Those who are spied upon may never even find out. In fact, there is no obligation to notify an individual that they have been subjected to surveillance once an investigation is closed.” Gallus concludes. “Furthermore, while the surveillance tools must be deactivated at the end of an operation, the material collected is not automatically deleted; instead, it may remain stored in the public prosecutor’s archives.”
